en: Compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhi of Changshui, Part Two:
Refuting Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra’s Attachment to Characteristics to Clarify Nature and Reveal the Tathāgatagarbha. Section Four: One, Presenting the Request.
Subsection Three: One, Summarizing What Remains Unresolved. Sub-subsection One: Paying Homage and Offering Praise.

At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra rose from his seat amidst the great assembly, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"O World-Honored One of Great Majestic Virtue!
"May you skillfully expound for the sake of sentient beings the Tathāgata’s ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
When the Tathāgata preached the Dharma, the great assembly sat together; those who wished to ask a question would first rise and pay their respects.
The ritual for expressing reverence does not depart from the three karmas:
kneeling with the right knee on the ground and joining the palms is the body; maintaining a reverent mind is the mind; [and speaking words of praise is the speech].
The phrase "spoke thus" refers to the mouth.
The Tathāgatagarbha-mind is neither empty nor existent; it is both essence and appearance, and is called the Ultimate Truth (paramārtha).
This is what the Buddha has realized; it is definitively free from delusion, and being thoroughly real, it is called the Truth (satya).
2. Quoting a Simile to Describe Delusion:

"World-Honored One, you have always declared that among those who expound the Dharma, I am the foremost. Yet now, hearing the subtle and wondrous sound of the Tathāgata’s Dharma, it is as if a deaf person were trying to listen for the sound of a mosquito from more than a hundred paces away; since they cannot see it at all, how much less could they hear it?"
"Although the Buddha has proclaimed and clarified this for me to eliminate my delusions, I have not yet fully understood the ultimate meaning of this principle to the point of being free from doubt.

Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra was skilled in expounding the essentials of the Dharma, and the assembly ranked him as unsurpassed; yet, having now heard the Buddha’s teaching, he has not yet fully grasped it. It is like a person with impaired hearing who, when faced with a subtle sound at a distance of more than a hundred paces, how could they possibly discern it clearly?
The ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is subtle, wondrous, and tranquil; it is a faint sound.
To hear it and yet not understand it is equivalent to not hearing it at all, like one who is deaf.
Where the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity ceases, it is as if one has gone beyond a hundred paces.
The teaching of these dharmas has caused me to eliminate my delusions; yet, as I am still ensnared by doubt and have not fully severed the knots of regret, I therefore employ this analogy.
Second, the comparative discussion of gain and loss.
“World-Honored One!
Although those such as Ānanda have attained awakening, their habitual outflows have not yet been eliminated.

As for us who have ascended to the state of being free from outflows within this assembly, though we have exhausted all taints, even now, upon hearing the Dharma-sound preached by the Tathāgata, we still harbor lingering doubts and regrets.”
"Awakening" refers to regaining the wondrous fundamental mind as previously described, which abides eternally and is indestructible.

In the Śrāvaka vehicle, those still in training (śaikṣa) have only severed the discriminative [afflictions], while the innate [afflictions] remain entirely; thus it is said that their habitual outflows have not yet been eliminated.
"Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, the unlearned (aśaikṣa) has completely severed all innate [afflictions]; this is said with reference to the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) of the Hīnayāna.
Question:

Why is it that even those who have attained the stage of no-more-learning still experience lingering doubt and regret, while those at the level of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) understand and awaken without doubt?"
Answer:

Due to the distinctions between the two obstacles—the afflictive and the cognitive—and the differing degrees of gravity between the grasping at a self of persons and the grasping at phenomena, the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states: "In some cases regarding an object, wisdom may be inferior to ignorance."
"It is said that while ordinary beings are well-versed in the Tripitaka, Arhats do not recognize red salt.

This is because the cognitive obscuration (jñeyāvaraṇa) obstructs the principle of the Dharmadhātu; thus, although Arhats have attained the untainted state (anāsrava), their afflictions are light, yet they still experience lingering doubt and regret because their cognitive obscurations are heavy.
Although Ānanda had attained awakening, what he knew was slight;
his habitual outflows were not yet eliminated, and thus his afflictions remained heavy.
Second, a detailed account of the doubts raised, in two parts:
1. Doubt regarding the arising aspect of the *tathāgatagarbha*:
"World-Honored One!

If all worldly faculties, objects, aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are the pure and original *tathāgatagarbha*, how is it that the various conditioned phenomena of mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise, undergoing successive transformations and flowing on, ending only to begin again?"
The first five phrases cite what has been heard, which is identical to Vajragarbha’s statement in the *Awakening of Faith*:
"If all sentient beings have been originally enlightened."
How should the following five phrases be understood as expressing a doubt and objection? They correspond to that [text] which asks:
"For what reason is there furthermore 'all-ignorance' (*sarvāvidyā*)?
That [text] then raises a counter-objection, saying:
"If all sentient beings inherently possess ignorance from the beginning, for what cause and condition does the Tathāgata further say that they have been enlightened from the very outset?
This objection does not appear in the present sutra because its meaning is already implicitly contained therein.

Furthermore, there is the method of restating [the objection] and then granting it while charging [the opponent] with infinite faults; this is identical to the separate responses to contradictions and hindrances found in the subsequent text.
Nevertheless, the questions posed by Vajragarbha form a series of successive difficulties, which are gathered together in this passage and linked like a chain.
The Tathāgata’s response to Śakra also provides a general indication, saying:

"The beginning and end of the world continue in succession from moment to moment; all dualities arise from the deluded perceptions of saṃsāra produced by the defiled mind of discrimination. Failing to leave behind these deluded perceptions while attempting to discern the nature of awakening, one consequently causes the nature of awakening to become subject to various cycles of transmigration."
The passage concludes by stating:
"Such distinctions do not constitute a correct question.

Now, since the questions in this sutra occur both earlier and later, the answers likewise follow those questions; although the two sutras differ in the breadth or brevity of their responses, their essential purport is the same.
As that sutra states:

"All various acts of grasping and rejecting are entirely within saṃsāra; to attempt to discern perfect enlightenment (圆觉) while not yet having emerged from saṃsāra is for that nature of perfect enlightenment to likewise undergo the cycle of transmigration. There is no way to avoid saṃsāra [in such a manner]. And so forth.

This is a reprimand of Gangzang for failing to understand that the self-nature of Perfect Enlightenment transcends all dualities, such that birth-and-death and nirvana are like a dream from yesterday; he has instead cited ignorance, birth-and-death, and conditioned phenomena to repeatedly raise doubts, thereby challenging the fact that sentient beings are originally enlightened Buddhas.

Therefore, the Buddha rejected this as being precisely the defiled mind of birth and death and the deluded views of discrimination, which ultimately cause Perfect Enlightenment to become the cycle of transmigration. For this reason, he employed metaphors such as "the clouds move and the moon moves" and "the boat travels and the shore shifts."

Now, this sutra takes what has been constantly taught—the essence of the nature of awakening, wondrously luminous and wondrously subtle—and turns it back to reprove [Pūrṇa], thereby distinguishing the minds of Māmatīputra’s understanding and delusion.

If one understands, one already knows that the essence of awakening is fundamentally wondrous, that ignorance is fundamentally empty, and that mountains, rivers, and the great earth are like the appearance of flowers in the sky; how then could there be any cause for doubt or confusion?

Thus, subject and object are falsely divided, and forced awareness suddenly arises; with the three subtleties as the root, the four wheels form the realms, and thereupon come into being the worlds, sentient beings, karmic fruits, and their continuities—all of these fail to transcend saṃsāra while attempting to discern Perfect Enlightenment. That nature of Perfect Enlightenment would then be identical to the cycle of transmigration.
Therefore, the intent of these two sutras is identical in both question and answer.

Nevertheless, this constitutes a major point of doubt and difficulty within the gateway of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), which most severely obstructs cultivation and realization. Although Pūrṇa’s outward appearance was that of a minor sage, his description of perfect penetration and his account of awakening in this sutra are entirely consistent with the Great Path; thus, the difficulties he presented are no different from those raised by Vajragarbha. May students who reach this point examine them closely.
2. Doubt regarding the simultaneous pervasiveness of their great nature:
"Furthermore, as the Tathāgata has said, the fundamental natures of earth, water, fire, and wind are perfectly interfused, pervading the entire Dharma-realm, serene and eternally abiding."
World-Honored One!
If the nature of earth were all-pervasive, how could it accommodate water?
If the nature of water were all-pervasive, fire would not arise.
Furthermore, how do you explain that the two natures of water and fire both pervade empty space without one subduing or extinguishing the other?
World-Honored One!
The nature of earth is obstructive, while the nature of space is vacuous and penetrating; how can these two both be all-pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm?

This refers to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) where the natures of water and fire differ; it challenges the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), wherein nature and characteristics are both fused.
The subsequent text answers: "When observing characteristics, they are fundamentally illusory and cannot be pointed out;
when observing nature, it is fundamentally true—nothing but wondrous, enlightened clarity."
"The wondrous, enlightened, and luminous mind was originally neither water nor fire; why then do you ask about the meaning of their mutual subjugation and extinction?
Third, the dual conclusion requesting instruction:
"I do not know where this principle leads; I only pray that the Tathāgata will spread forth his great compassion to dispel the clouds of delusion for me and for this great assembly."
Having spoken these words, he prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, thirsting for the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed compassionate instruction.
"You" (yōu) means "that which.
According to the teaching, it is fundamentally pure, mutually pervasive, and mutually interfused.
According to what we see now, mountains and rivers appear vividly present, yet they utterly contradict the nature of water and fire.
We do not know where they have gone; who is right and who is wrong? I pray that you will deign to grant us compassionate instruction, so that we may hope to be free from delusion.
II. Granting the Teaching, in three parts:
A. Introduction to the Exposition.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Pūrṇa and all the Arhats in the assembly who were taintless and had attained the stage of no-more-learning:
"Today, the Tathāgata universally proclaims for this assembly the true nature of the ultimate within the ultimate.
The Tathāgata always teaches the Dharma by relying upon the two truths, namely, the conventional truth and the ultimate truth.
What is now being expounded differs from conventional teachings; it refers to the ultimate among ultimates, the ultimate truth.

Within the single true *dharmadhātu*, the middle way of real mark, there is no phenomenon that is not subsumed and no phenomenon that is not pervaded. From the highest sages to the lowest ordinary beings, and including both sentient and insentient things, all attain the Buddha-way. This is the supreme proclamation and the final model left behind.
2. Manifesting the Benefits:

"It shall cause those in your assembly who are śrāvakas of fixed nature, as well as all those arhats who have not yet attained the two kinds of emptiness but have turned toward the Mahāyāna, to all obtain the ground of quiescent extinction of the One Vehicle—the true site of *araṇya* for correct practice."

The expedient teachings state that those of fixed nature among the two vehicles and the icchantikas who lack the Buddha-nature cannot attain Buddhahood, being likened to scorched sprouts or rotten seeds.
Now, this assembly reconciles these views, so that all return to the One Vehicle and reach ultimate nirvana.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "In other sūtras, I have said that there are śrāvakas who cannot become buddhas; it is not in this sūtra that I speak thus.
Since nirvāṇa and buddha-nature are the tathāgatagarbha, which is also called the One Vehicle and the Śūraṅgama, is it not fitting that these two sūtras share the same flavor?
This, then, synthesizes the five natures and harmonizes the three vehicles; as the ultimate discourse on definitive meaning, nothing surpasses it.
"Āraṇya" means being free from clamor and distraction.
The "Śūraṅgama King" is the great samādhi of all Buddhas, named the true place for practice where there is no clamor or distraction.
3. Command to Listen:
"Listen now attentively; I shall speak for you. 3. Waiting to Hear.
Pūrṇa and the others, revering the Buddha’s Dharma-voice, listened in silence.
Fourth, the response and explanation, in two parts:
first, answering the doubt regarding the characteristics of arising within the storehouse nature (ālaya-gotra), in two parts: [1] the response itself; [2] the subsequent explanation.
I. Directly answering the doubt, in three parts:
A. Restating the doubt.
The Buddha said:
“Pūrṇa! As you have said, [the nature of reality] is fundamentally pure; how then could mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise?
2. The direct answer, in two parts:
1. The Single True Mind.
“Have you not always heard the Tathāgata proclaim that the nature of awareness is wondrously luminous, and that fundamental awareness is luminously wondrous? Pūrṇa replied:
“Yes, indeed, World-Honored One!
I have constantly heard the Buddha proclaim this meaning.

The one true suchness-mind is what the Buddha constantly speaks of; it is sometimes called the *dharmadhātu*, sometimes called the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), sometimes called the *tathāgatagarbha*-nature, and sometimes called the wondrously pure and luminous mind.
If even within a single sutra there are many names, how much more so across all the sutras?
Although the names differ, the essence is one and without distinction; they all reveal the single characteristic of the dharma-realm, which is fundamentally equal.

The three categories and seven elements are falsely born and falsely extinguished; yet birth and extinction, coming and going, are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha—unmoving and all-pervasive, the wondrous nature of True Suchness. Within this true, eternal nature, one seeks in vain for coming and going, delusion and enlightenment, or birth and death, for nothing at all can be found.
If one thoroughly understands this principle, why would mountains and rivers suddenly arise, or why would conditioned phenomena undergo flux?
Why, then, would there be any need to pose questions to the Tathāgata?
Thus, these inquiries have already resolved all doubts; this response is given from the perspective of the *tathatā* gate, defining the essence as being utterly devoid of characteristics.
"Nature-awareness" (*xingjue*) and "original awareness" (*benjue*) refer to the essence (*ti*).
"Wondrous luminosity" (*miaoming*) and "luminous wondrousness" (*mingmiao*) manifest the function (*yong*).
Since this manifestation does not depend on another, it is called "nature-awareness": because nature is inherently aware and nature is inherently luminous, how could it depend on another?

It is called "original enlightenment" (benjue) because it reveals that there is no beginning; since it is enlightened from the outset and luminous from the outset, how could it exist as a result of a beginning?
Furthermore, its essence is immutable, hence it is called "intrinsic enlightenment" (xingjue);
its characteristics do not arise, hence it is called "original enlightenment."
Its essence and characteristics are quiescent and extinguished, beyond the reach of mind and speech; therefore, it is called "wondrous.
Its spiritual discernment is never obscured, and no delusion can darken it; therefore, it is named "luminous."
"Wondrous clarity" and "clarity that is wondrous" are merely different ways of speaking about the same thing.

Alternatively, it may be called "wondrous clarity" because it is quiescent yet constantly illuminating, and "clarity that is wondrous" because it is illuminating yet constantly quiescent; this reveals that the Dharma-realm has but a single characteristic, and true awakening is non-dual.
The *Awakening of Mahāśrī* (*Yuánjué*) also states: "Because all things are awakening, universal awakening shines everywhere; it is quiescent extinction, without duality.
The interpretations offered by ancients each followed their own inclinations; such details are left to them, as I cannot recount them all here.
2. Second, the arising of all delusive phenomena is explained by way of the gate of birth-and-death (*utpāda-nirodha-dvāra*) as it forms events in accordance with conditions.
This section has three parts:
first, a general inquiry regarding enlightened clarity (*jue-ming*).
The Buddha said:

"When you refer to 'awakened clarity,' does this mean that the nature itself is clear and thus called 'awakening,' or does it mean that awakening is not inherently clear and thus called 'clear awakening'?"

This single question is intended to determine whether one has attained understanding or remains in delusion. If one has attained understanding, there would be no cause for doubt; if one is deluded, this cannot be considered a correct question.
The intent of the question is:
"Upon hearing me speak of the wondrous clarity of the nature of awareness, what interpretation do you form?"
Is it that the essential nature of this awakening is inherently luminous, and thus called "awakening-luminosity"?
Or is it that awakening itself is not luminous, but because it perceives the luminosity of others, this luminosity—which is distinct from awakening—is called "luminous-awakening"?
By whom was the title "Awakened Clarity" (Jue-ming) established?
Therefore, it says, "You call it... and so forth.
Regarding these two meanings—one correct and one erroneous—it remains for Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra to determine which meaning he intends in his response.

Attaining this brings about freedom from doubt, whereas recognizing what is false gives rise to delusion; therefore, this single question is intended to definitively distinguish between understanding and delusion.
Second, the answer is based on that which is perceived. Pūrṇa said:
"If this lack of illumination were itself called awakening, then there would be nothing illuminated.
According to the meaning of this response, the essence of awakening cannot illuminate itself; it must necessarily rely on another, external illumination to serve as its object of awakening.
If there were no luminosity that serves as the object of awakening, it could only be called "awakening" alone and could not be termed "awakening-luminosity.

If one wishes to term it "awakening-luminosity," there must necessarily be luminosity as the object of awakening; this would merely be to identify with the false and take it as the source from which deluded phenomena arise.

The Buddha’s fundamental intent is that the nature of awakening is primordially luminous; it does not become luminous and awakened by depending on anything else. Awakening is wondrously luminous, and its wondrous luminosity is wondrous;

awakening is perfect luminosity, and its perfect luminosity is perfect. Luminous awakening is a single mark, without duality or distinction. This is solely true awakening, with no other dharma; apart from this single jewel-mark, everything else is the work of demons.
Pūrṇa initiates the teaching by demonstrating that he himself was unaware, having mistakenly identified what he perceived as true, thereby falling into delusion and confusion.
Third, the section on "Enumerating Delusions through Calculation" has two parts;
first, the provisional refutation of Pūrṇa’s dualistic attachments regarding subject and object, which has three sub-sections:
First, destroying true awakening causes one to fall into the duality of subject and object.
The Buddha said:
"If there is nothing to be enlightened, then there is no enlightenment; if there is something [to be enlightened], it is not awakening."
The first two phrases collectively cite the [opponent's] conceptualization.

If you maintain that there must be something illuminated for it to be called "illuminating awareness," and that if there is nothing illuminated there can be no "illuminating awareness," the Buddha then refutes this by saying:
"That which has an object is not true awareness."
The meaning is this:
if there were subject and object, how could it be called true awakening?
For true awakening is free from the characteristics of subject and object.

The verse on the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) states: "When, with respect to the object of cognition, wisdom finds nothing at all to be apprehended, at that time one abides in *vijñaptimātra*, because one is free from the characteristics of the two grasps.
A sūtra says: "If one does not understand the mind and its objects, then the two types of false conceptualization arise;
if one understands the mind and its spheres, false conceptualization does not arise."
The preceding passage states: "The awareness of what is perceived is a cataract; awareness itself is not within the cataract.
Thus, one knows that the existence of an object is not true awareness.
Second, the refutation of the wondrous nature as being neither tranquil nor luminous.
"There is nothing that is not the object of illumination, yet ignorance is not the nature of the profound clarity of awakening.
The first phrase specifically cites the object of illumination.

If it were as you say—that there must be an object of illumination for it to be called "awakened illumination," and that if there were no object of illumination it could only be called "awakening"—then the next two phrases refute this:
The Tathāgata has always taught that the nature of awakening is profoundly still and luminous; how could it be ignorance?
If it were truly ignorance, it would not be fitting to call it the nature of profound stillness and luminosity.
Third, this concludes by demonstrating the two types of awakening: the true and the deluded.
"The nature-awareness must be luminous; delusion constitutes its luminous awareness.
The first phrase concludes the discussion on the True, while the second concludes the discussion on the Delusive.
Since the nature-awareness necessarily possesses true luminosity, it is said that "the nature-awareness is wondrously luminous" and "original awareness is luminously wondrous."
You falsely claim that illumination is distinct from awareness; therefore, you say:

"If there were nothing to be illuminated, then there would be no illuminating awareness, for it is only by virtue of having something to be illuminated that one can speak of 'illuminating awareness.'"
The distinction between delusion and enlightenment can thus be discerned.
Second, the correct elucidation of the causes by which delusion arises from the True: this has two parts.
First, a general clarification of the manner in which deluded awareness relies upon the True.
"Awareness is not that which is illumined; it is because of illumination that an object is established.

The essence of true awareness is inherently endowed with wondrous clarity; it does not arise following conditions nor is it produced by objects. It is fundamentally quiescent and illuminating, a single mark throughout the dharma-realm; therefore, it is said that "awareness is not that which is illumined."

Therefore, because true illumination is not understood due to ignorance, one falsely clings to it as an object; thus, as soon as a single thought arises, the four delusions arise simultaneously, and there is no initial manifestation of the fundamental consciousness that is not of this nature.
The *Awakening of Faith* states: "Because one does not know, as they truly are, that the dharma of True Suchness is one, the mind arises through non-awakening and possesses thought.
It further states: "That which is neither identical to nor different from the union of the unborn and undying with the arising and ceasing is called the ālayavijñāna."
This true luminosity is established as the "object of illumination" (so-ming) because it is apprehended by grasping.

This is precisely True Suchness (tathatā) which, failing to maintain its own nature, becomes the "characterized object" (so-xiang) when perceived by delusion; it is like the light of a lamp which, when seen through a cataract, appears as a circular halo. This is called the ignorance of the beginningless dwelling-ground (anādikālika-ālaya-avidyā).
The *Śrīmaladevī-siṃhanāda Sūtra* states: "Prior to the four stages of abiding (*catur-vihāra-bhūmi*), no afflictions (*anuśaya*) arise; therefore, they are quiescent and extremely subtle.
This refers precisely to that which is characterized [by these stages].
Second, a detailed analysis of how the three characteristics arise sequentially, in two parts:
I. Establishing the characteristics of the reason (hetu-lakṣaṇa), in two parts:
A. Specifically showing the three characteristics, in three parts:
1. The characteristic of difference (vaidharmya).
"Once the object has been falsely established, it gives rise to your false subjectivity; within that which is devoid of identity or difference, a blazing diversity is formed.
This is what the *Awakening of Faith* calls the "phase of karma" (*karmalakṣaṇa*); thus the treatise states: "Because of reliance on non-awakening, the mind moves; this is designated as karma."
When there is awakening, there is no movement; when there is movement, there is suffering, because the fruit does not deviate from its cause.
As for this sutra being called "Diverse Characteristics" (*nānātva-lakṣaṇa*), "diversity" has two meanings:
first, diversity is discussed in terms of mutual comparison, meaning that non-awakening leads to movement while awakening leads to non-movement; thus, movement is different from non-movement.

Second is the distinction based on their essential nature (*tattva*). This means that this karma possesses both the subjective capacity (*karana*) and the objective object (*karman*), and it is subject to arising and ceasing.
When this text now states, "Since the object has been falsely established, you have falsely given rise to the subject," it refers precisely to this distinction based on essential nature.

True awakening is wondrously luminous and fundamentally lacks the characteristics of subject and object; yet, through the lack of awareness of ignorance, it is falsely perceived as an object. Because this false object is established, a false subject arises accordingly; thus, the two minds of subject and object do not exist apart from one another.
Regarding "that which blazes forth as difference within the absence of identity and difference," this refers to the discussion of difference in mutual relation.
Since the essence of the single truth is free from the characteristics of verbal expression and free from the characteristics of mental conditioning, there is neither identity nor difference.
The false distinction between subject and object suddenly gives rise to two aspects; these are clearly established as being distinct from the aspectless.
This is also called the "aspect of movement," because it differs from the quiescent mind.
2. Common Characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
"That which differs from what is differentiated is established as common based on its difference.

In the *Awakening of Faith*, this is termed the "evolving characteristic" (*vivarta-lakṣaṇa*); thus the treatise states: "Because it relies on movement, there is seeing; if there were no movement, there would be no seeing."
"Transformation" (pariṇāma) means arising; it refers to the arising of the previously moving mind, which constitutes the capacity for seeing.

What is now called "different from that which is differentiated" (tasmād anyat) means that the differentiator is the common characteristic (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa), while the differentiated is the specific characteristic (viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa).
If one wishes to distinguish between different characteristics, one must establish the name "sameness.
What was previously different from the "real" is now different from the "different"; it is in dependence upon the "different" that "sameness" is established;
furthermore, it is because [sameness] is coarse and manifest.
It is also called the characteristic of stillness (*śānta-lakṣaṇa*), because stillness differs from movement.
This stillness exists in relation to movement; it is not an absolute stillness independent of all else. Therefore, it is said that "sameness is established based on difference.
Third, the characteristic of neither sameness nor difference (*na-samāna-na-viṣama-lakṣaṇa*).
"From the manifestation of identity and difference, there further arises the establishment of neither identity nor difference.
The *Awakening of Faith* calls this the "manifestation of signs," and thus the treatise states: "Because it relies upon the capacity for seeing, objects falsely appear;
apart from seeing, there are no objects."
This refers to the manifestation of the three objects within the *ālaya-vijñāna*.

As for the present statement regarding "the manifestation of identity and difference," it is because the two prior characteristics of identity and difference manifest through mutual contrast; consequently, the mental characteristics become increasingly coarse and are able to constitute external objects. This name is established in relation to those two preceding [characteristics]: it is called "non-identity" (*asama*) not because it is the prior characteristic of stillness, and it is called "non-difference" (*abheda*) not because it is the prior characteristic of movement.

This refers to the absence of identity and difference within the context of relative identity and difference, rather than the absolute negation of identity and difference; thus it is said that "identity and difference are manifested.

These three characteristics are the limits of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*); their continuous flow and arising-and-perishing ceaselessly persist from moment to moment, such that they cannot be awakened to by ordinary beings or those of the Two Vehicles.

Arising from that single moment of ignorance, the *Awakening of Faith* calls it "non-associated defilement" (*asamprayukta-kleśa*), which only a Buddha can fully exhaust. Thus the text says: "The consciousness arising from the perfuming of ignorance cannot be known by ordinary beings, nor can it be realized by the wisdom of the two vehicles; rather, it is through the observation initiated by a Bodhisattva’s initial resolve based on right faith that one attains partial knowledge upon realizing the Dharma-body. Even at the ultimate stage of a Bodhisattva, it cannot be fully known; only a Buddha comprehends it thoroughly."
2. General Summary and Explanation:
"Such disturbances, in mutual dependence, give rise to weariness; this weariness, prolonged, gives rise to dust, which naturally becomes turbid.

Thus, these three elements mutually disturb and vex one another, and through their constant mutual intermingling, form and dependency never cease, eventually resulting in exhaustion—just as when the eyes are fatigued, there appear illusory flowers before them.
The three characteristics falsely defile the true nature; therefore, they are called "dust" (*rajas*).
They turbid the pure essence, causing its luminous clarity to be lost; therefore, they are called "turbidity.
There are five levels of coarse and subtle names and characteristics of this turbidity, as will be extensively analyzed below; all of them take these three as their fundamental basis.
II. Distinguishing the characteristics of the fruit, in two parts:
A. The drawing forth of the fruit by means of causes, in two parts:
1. The drawing forth of the coarse by means of the subtle.
"From this, the dust-like afflictions (*kleśa*) are incited.

This means that from the three preceding subtle states, the four coarse states are incited—namely, the mark of cognition (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*), its continuity, grasping, and the conceptualization of names.

These four are precisely the substance of the two obstacles; because they arise only when the internal perfuming of false conceptualization and the external perfuming of objective realms are fully present as causes and conditions, they are said to "give rise to" them.
Defiled toil, the performance of karma and the undergoing of its retribution, and the endless cycle of transmigration—all stem from this; it is the path of afflictions (*kleśa-mārga*).
Inferior karmic fruits and sentient beings correspond to the latter two types of coarseness.
The *Awakening of Faith* states: "Because there are objective conditions, six kinds of characteristics further arise.
These are the six coarse [characteristics].
Second, the internal evokes the external.

“Arising constitutes the world, while stillness constitutes empty space. Empty space is characterized by sameness, whereas the world is characterized by difference; yet in that which is neither same nor different, there are truly no conditioned phenomena.”
Arising is movement; movement is the characteristic of change (*anyathātva*). Change is termed differentiation, which constitutes the substance of the world (*loka-dhātu*).

"World" (*loka*) refers to flux and transition, while "realm" (*dhātu*) refers to spatial orientation. Because they undergo successive transformations and are distinct and separate, they are called the "world-realm. All of these take internal differentiation as their fundamental basis; therefore, it is said that arising constitutes the world-realm.
Quiescence is the same aspect; being the same, it is called "not different. Because form involves distinctions and agitation, quiescence is named as such; it is the very substance of empty space.

Space has no distinctions or shifting movements; because it possesses the internal same aspect, which serves as the cause for the quiescence that stands in contrast to movement, it is said that "quiescence constitutes empty space."
The two lines following "empty space" conclude [the discussion] by means of the two characteristics.

The passage beginning with "that which is non-existent" points to the manifest characteristic; it is also called the manifest consciousness (*nirbhāsa-vijñāna*). This refers to the stage where the three characteristics of the *ālaya* are fully accomplished, and is therefore termed a truly conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), because it is capable of accomplishing the eight consciousnesses, the six sense objects, the sense organs, the body, the seeds, and so forth.

Although the first two characteristics are also conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), because the three characteristics are not yet complete and their functional efficacy has not been fulfilled, they are only designated as "conditioned" at the stage of their full accomplishment.

Furthermore, this single characteristic is called "without sameness or difference. Since this could be confused with the previously mentioned essence of true suchness (*tathatā*) and awakening, which are also without sameness or difference, this term specifically indicates that it refers to conditioned phenomena; thus, one knows it is not the truly non-differentiated [unconditioned].
There is no distinction between identity and difference, as both the true and the false exist together; by means of this discrimination, there is no loss of confusion between them.

Although these three characteristics are described in a sequential order, their arising is simultaneous. The external vessel-world, space, and the sense faculties of sentient beings that they induce all manifest instantaneously in a single thought-moment; they do not occur one after another. One must not, therefore, demand a sequence in their manifestation based on the order in which they were described.
II. The explicit explanation of the characteristics of the result, in three parts:
A. The continuity of the world-system, in two parts:
1. Discerning its characteristics, in two parts:
First, explaining the arising of the four wheels, in four parts:
First, the wind wheel.
"Awakened clarity and empty darkness interact to produce agitation; thus there is the wind wheel that sustains the world."
Because what was previously falsely established gave rise to your false capacity.

The "object" (so) is the shadow of light, and the "subject" (neng) is false awareness; this awareness-illumination is entirely ignorance (*avidyā*). This ignorance, dull and dark, pervades the entire dharma-realm and thus constitutes empty obscurity.

Therefore, the subsequent text states: "You perceive empty space pervading the realms of the ten directions; space and perception are not distinguished," and so forth. Here, "perception" refers to deluded cognition.

One clarity and one obscurity, one movement and one stillness, arise and perish in each instant, interacting without ceasing. This internal arising and perishing is termed "shaking"; externally, it constitutes the initial emergence of the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*). Thus, at the beginning of the world, the wind-circle is primary, and empty space serves as the support for the world.
Therefore, the subsequent passage states: "From delusion there arises empty space; based upon space, the world is established.

Second, the Golden Wheel: "Because of space, movement arises; from the firmness of clarity, obstruction is established. That golden treasure is the firmness established by luminous awareness; thus, the Golden Wheel exists to sustain the land."
Because the arising and ceasing of ignorance are in constant mutual dependence, it is said that "shaking arises from emptiness.
Because one clings to what is perceived as clarity and maintains it firmly without relinquishing it, it is said that "obstruction is established upon firm clarity."

Internally, this is the firm attachment to enlightened clarity; externally, it manifests as the golden wheel that arises next. Therefore, it is said: "That precious gold is the firm establishment of enlightened clarity.
Thus we know that the nature of the jewel exists because of enlightened clarity; for this reason, all jewels are solid in essence and luminous in function.
3. The Fire-Wheel.
"The solid perception is formed from jewels; when shaken by the wind of luminosity, the wind and the metal rub against each other, thus producing fire-light, which has transformation as its nature."
The first two lines refer to the first two natures, which serve as the cause for the production of fire.

Internally, there is incessant arising and ceasing, characterized by stubborn attachment and refusal to let go; externally, there is unceasing movement and vibration, characterized by hardness and resistance to destruction. Through their mutual friction, fire is produced—just as in the method of kindling fire, where the fire-drill and the wood are one firm and one moving.
Fire can melt and disperse, bringing all things to maturity; therefore, it is said to have the nature of transformation.
Fourth, the water wheel:
"The brilliance of the jewels produces moisture, and the fire-light steams upward from above; thus there is a water wheel that contains the worlds of the ten directions."

Internally, there is the firm attachment to craving and clear light, and the parched mind is intensely aflame; externally, there is the moistening by jewels and the steaming by fire, which consequently forms flowing water.
Just as when worldly objects are steamed there must be dirty runoff, so too no seeds of karma arise without craving, and no grasses or trees grow without water.

Because these four natures mutually depend upon one another, their essences are not separate, as they are all equally produced by the transformations of the deluded mind; they are like flowers in the sky, which do not exist apart from the visual impairment.
Fools do not understand this; because they hold inverted views, they grasp at objects as existing apart from the mind.

However, the Hīnayāna schools place the water-circle before the gold-circle, which differs from this [Mahāyāna] view; yet they fail to realize that the wind-circle supporting the water is itself solid and obstructive.
The characteristics are discussed later while the nature is presented first; therefore, immediately after the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*), the gold-circle (*kāñcana-maṇḍala*) is explained.

Furthermore, those [beings] only know that it is produced by predominant karma (*adhipati-karman*), yet they do not know its causal seed (*hetu-bīja*), because this teaching is of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*) and describes only coarse characteristics.
Second, the manifestation of various characteristics is explained:
"Fire ascends and water descends; their mutual interaction establishes solidity. The moisture becomes the vast ocean, and the dryness becomes the continents and sandbars.
For this reason, within that great ocean, flames constantly arise, and within those continents and sandbars, rivers and streams constantly flow."
The flames ascend and seek the dry, while the water descends and flows to moisten; as they strike against one another, they immediately form solid obstructions.
Although fire ascends and strikes back, it is ultimately overcome by water; therefore, the great ocean is vast while the sandbanks and islets are narrow.

All arise from the delusive nature being impermanent and subject to change between before and after: because the mind of attachment is abundant, it forms a vast ocean; because the mind of grasping is intense, it forms islands and sandbanks.

From the nature of anger arises pride, and from the nature of grasping arises anger; when love for form arises, water flows through the midst of the sandbanks, and when aversion toward love arises, fire erupts within the ocean.
That which can be inhabited within water is called an island (*dvīpa*); that which is a mound of sand within water is called a sandbar (*taraṅga*).
"The power of water is inferior to fire; it solidifies into high mountains. Therefore, when the rocks of these mountains are struck, they produce flames, and when melted, they become water."
Externally, the power of water is inferior to that of fire; internally, hatred increases while love diminishes.
When hatred is further compounded by pride, they coalesce into a high mountain.

The power of earth is inferior to that of water; it is drawn forth as grass and trees. Therefore, when forests and thickets encounter fire, they become earth, and through compression, they become water.
Externally, the power of the earth is inferior to that of water; internally, craving increases while pride becomes light.
Craving can produce water, and water can nourish and cause the sprouts of grasses and trees to grow.
Hatred, craving, and pride—these three mutually proliferate and take form as distinct categories, resulting in the myriad differences of plants, trees, mountains, and rivers.
Second, the binding of continuity.
"Mutual delusions arise and serve as seeds for one another; by these causes and conditions, the world continues in succession.

First, from the agitation between clarity and obscurity, there arises the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*). From the wind agitating the clarity, the precious metal [the earth] is established. The mutual friction of gold and wind gives rise to the nature of fire. The fire steams the moisture of the gold, giving rise to water. When water and fire interact, their forces vary in strength and weakness: where water prevails and fire is weak, there are oceans and islands; where fire prevails and water is weak, there are mountains and rocks; where earth is weak and water prevails, there are plants, trees, and the like.
Although external phenomena appear thus, they all arise from the internal mind;
if the internal mind undergoes no change, how could there be any differentiation externally?
Since the sutra speaks here in terms of the external, it says that they act as seeds for one another.
II. The Continuity of Sentient Beings, in two parts: A.
Distinguishing its characteristics, in two parts: 1.
Clarifying the initial formation of the faculties and objects, in two parts: [text continues]
First, pointing back to the characteristics of the cause:
"Furthermore, Pūrṇa! That ignorance within clarity is not caused by another;
the fault lies in the awakening-clarity itself. Once that which is falsely established exists, the principle of clarity cannot transcend it."

"Clarity" (ming) means manifestation. This manifestation of delusion does not arise from any other external condition; it occurs solely because of one's own single thought-moment of non-comprehension, whereby the subject and object are falsely divided, resulting in this fault. Thus, "awakened clarity" (jue-ming) is precisely this subject-object duality.

Since the illumination that has been clarified is already established, it gives rise to the cognizing mind, which continues in a succession of moments such that one cannot be separated from thought. Consequently, the wondrous principle of true illumination is obstructed by these thoughts; it remains hidden and is set aside, unable to transcend them and manifest.
2. Conclusion on the Formation of Faculties and Objects:

"For these reasons and conditions, hearing does not transcend sound, and seeing does not go beyond form; thus the six delusions of form, fragrance, taste, and touch are established, whereby seeing, sensing, hearing, and knowing become separated."

Ignorance (*avidyā*) serves as the cause, and that which is illuminated [by it] serves as the condition; through their mutual interaction, they reach a state where there is neither identity nor difference. From within this single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*), the faculties (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*) emerge.

Once the faculties and objects have coincided, consciousness (*vijñāna*) arises between them. These three—the faculty, the object, and consciousness—constitute the nature of karma; each respectively grasps and absorbs its own sphere without functioning through other conditions. Therefore, it is said that they do not transcend [this state].

Thus, from what was previously explained, the six sense objects are differentiated; and from the preceding false cognition, the functions of hearing, seeing, and so forth are opened up. It is for this reason that it was stated previously that the "luminous cognition" (*jue-ming*) is the fault.
II. Distinguishing the Primary Causes of the Classes of Beings, in two parts:
1. Citing the classes to provide a general indication:
"Bound together by common karma, their union and separation bring about transformation."
Sentient beings born from the womb or from eggs must depend on the mutual resonance of the karma of both parents; therefore, it is said that "mutual karma entangles them.

Sentient beings born from moisture or by transformation, however, depend only on the union or separation of their own mental conceptions: they are born from moisture where there is union, and born by transformation where there is separation. Since these do not depend on the mutual resonance of the karma of parents, it is said that "union and separation bring about transformation."
"Transformation" (*nirmāṇa*) is the general designation for that which arises, as all such things are termed "transformations.

Second, a detailed analysis according to their causes has two parts: first, the formation of seeds by grasping objects; second, [the formation of seeds] by grasping internal states. Regarding the first: [text follows].
First, the causes of feeling and perception: "When one sees brightness, color arises;
when one sees clearly, perception is formed. Different perceptions give rise to aversion; similar perceptions give rise to attachment.
Here, "seeing" refers to deluded seeing, and "brightness" is that which is made clear. Because of seeing, there is brightness; brightness is able to manifest color.
Because of causes and conditions, views arise; from views, perceptions are produced. When the object differs from the perception, this difference constitutes a contradiction, which leads to aversion.
When form is identical to the mind, this identity constitutes conformity, which consequently gives rise to attachment.

If there is difference, there is only ideation without craving; if there is similarity, ideation and craving proceed together. It is through this that one enters the womb, for which the requisites of ideation and craving are required.
Second, the formation of the species.
"The flow of craving serves as the seed, and the reception of perception serves as the womb; through their union, birth occurs, drawing in those of similar karma.
Thus, by means of causes and conditions, there arise the *kalala*, the *arbuda*, and so forth."

"Seed" refers to that which has already been moistened by craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*); it is the seed distinct from its original state, hence it is said that "the flow of craving constitutes the seed.

"Womb" (*garbha*) refers specifically to the moment when the single thought-moment of consciousness arises as actualized activity (*pravṛtti*). However, since both ideation (*saṃjñā*) and craving together constitute the seed, and both ideation and craving together constitute the womb, the sutra text employs abbreviation, citing only one of each.

The parents and the child share three states of emotional and conceptual affinity; they mutually unite and encounter one another, thereby triggering the absorption of shared karma from their respective realms and destinies. This causes them to converge into a single location, forming the fetal matrix; hence it is said that "through mutual union and encounter, shared karma is drawn forth."
One's own karma acts as the cause, while the three bases and the perception of a sentient being act as the conditions.
*Kalala* means "coagulated mucus.
*Arbuda* means "blister"; it refers to the first two weeks within the womb.
If the thirty-seven days are reached, the embryo and the egg are divided; therefore, the preceding two states are described as the undivided stage.
Second, they are divided into the four modes of birth:

"Womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born, according to what is appropriate for each. The egg-born arises solely through thought; the womb-born is due to emotional attachment; the moisture-born results from a response to union; and the transformation-born occurs through a response to separation."
Briefly stated, there are four modes of birth; in detail, there are twelve, as will be extensively analyzed below.
When the four modes of birth arise, one takes rebirth in accordance with the place where karma and mental dispositions correspond; therefore, it is said that "it follows what is appropriate."

The four modes of birth are all characterized by the union and separation of feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*); here, one example is cited for each based on their predominant characteristics, as the subsequent sutra itself contains various accounts regarding the relative abundance of feeling and perception.

Furthermore, among those born from an eggshell, the majority possess perception; because creatures such as birds, fish, and dragons are all swift in movement, they are said to be "born of perception."

Among those born from a womb, sentient beings have much conceptual thought and little emotion; because they have many emotions, they fall heavily and cannot rise lightly, hence it is said that "emotion exists.

Among those born from moisture, birth does not depend on parents; rather, through the mere union of one's own conceptual thought with the moist environment, one immediately undergoes birth, hence it is said that "union brings about [rebirth]."

Transformation [birth] also occurs when one spontaneously conceives an image or intensely visualizes a superior realm; through attachment to that object, one is immediately born by transformation, hence it is called "leaving behind the response" (liying).
Second, the linking of continuity.

“Affections and perceptions join and separate, constantly changing and transforming one another; all karmic retributions follow their ascent or descent. By these causes and conditions, sentient beings continue in succession.

Affections and perceptions are not constant, changing from moment to moment; they may first be born from a womb and later from an egg, or first from moisture and later through transformation. All received retributions follow the goodness or evil of one’s karma; therefore, it is said that they “follow their flight or submergence.”
Because there is no ability to sever the transition from one body to another, it is called the "continuity of sentient beings.
Third, the continuity of karmic results has two parts: first, the analysis of its characteristics, which has two [subdivisions]: [The text continues with the second subdivision.]
I. Correct Exposition, in three parts: A. The Root of Desire. "Pūrṇa!..."

When perception and craving are bound together and one cannot separate from craving, then the succession of parents and children throughout the world continues without end; these things have desire and greed as their root.
The depths of their craving and desire bind them to one another; being obstructed and difficult to relinquish, they are said to be "unseparated.
When parents give birth to a child, and that child in turn gives birth to a grandson, and so on through successive generations without interruption—all this has desire as its root.
2. The Root of Killing:

"When craving increases together with greed and greed cannot be restrained, then among all beings in the world—whether born from eggs, by transformation, from moisture, or from a womb—they devour one another according to their relative strength and weakness; these acts are rooted in the greed for killing."
"Killing for the sake of greed in order to nourish one's own life;
using force to oppress the weak so that the slaughter does not cease—this is the root of killing.
Third, the root of stealing."

"When humans eat sheep, the sheep die and become humans; when humans die, they become sheep. In this way, through ten successive lifetimes, as they die and are born again, they prey upon one another. Their evil karma arises together with them, persisting until the end of the future. Such beings take the greed for theft as their root."
To take what is not given is called theft.
Now, to consume the property of others through improper means is to seize their very lives.

Because of these evil karmas, beings are born together in the same world as enemies; they encounter one another to settle their debts, plundering each other incessantly until the end of the future, all of which has its root in theft.
2. Explanation and Confirmation:
"You owe me my life, and I shall repay you for your debt; by reason of this cause and condition, we shall remain constantly within birth and death for hundreds of thousands of kalpas."
This explains killing and stealing.
"You love my heart, and I cherish your beauty; because of these causes and conditions, for hundreds of thousands of kalpas we shall remain constantly bound in entanglement."
This explains the desire for sensual pleasure.
Third, the continuity of the stream:
"Only killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct constitute the roots; by these causes and conditions, the fruits of karma continue."
Killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct are the three actual courses of action; since all arise with craving as their condition, these three are all referred to as "greed."
Because the causal karma and the resultant suffering arise in succession without interruption, it is called "continuous.
Second, the conclusion of the answer: "Pūrṇa!..."

These three kinds of inverted continuities are all the nature of the luminous clarity of awareness that cognizes; because this cognition gives rise to appearances, the various conditioned phenomena of mountains, rivers, and the great earth arise from deluded vision. They flow and shift in succession, and through this falsehood, they end and begin again.
The wondrous substance of awakened clarity inherently possesses the nature of lucid knowing; this is precisely "the wondrous luminosity of the nature of awakening.

Because it is fundamentally lucid, one becomes deluded and creates that which is perceived—this is "establishing the object based on luminosity. Therefore, it is said: "Based on lucidity, the phenomenal aspect arises."
These characteristics arise from false discrimination; therefore, it is said they are born from deluded vision.

This summarizes the three types of continuity mentioned previously: all result from being deluded regarding the fundamental true luminosity, whereby the falsely constituted "characterized" (the object) necessarily gives rise to the "characterizer" (the subject). Through this progressive coarsening and attachment, the sequential flux of the world, sentient beings, and karmic fruits is established—all of which do not depart from the single thought-moment of ignorant, deluded awareness.
2. A specific response to objections, in two parts:
A. Pūrṇa raises a difficulty. Pūrṇa said:

"If this wondrous enlightenment is fundamentally wondrously enlightened and luminous, neither increasing nor decreasing compared to the Tathāgata’s mind, then why did the various conditioned phenomena of mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise without cause? Now that the Tathāgata has attained this wondrous, empty, and luminous enlightenment, when will the habitual taints of the conditioned mountains, rivers, and great earth ever arise again?"

"The wondrously enlightened, luminous mind is of the same substance as the Buddha; it is fundamentally without delusion. It is only because of forceful awareness that one suddenly identifies with perceived objects, whereby delusion arises.
Since the Buddha has now attained the wondrous, empty, and luminous mind, when could delusions ever suddenly arise again?"
This is to cite [the opponent's position] and then grant it [a conditional acceptance], thereby charging them with the fault of infinite regress.
It is the same as Vajragarbha saying:

"If ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) of the ten directions have fundamentally attained the Buddha-way, yet subsequently give rise to ignorance, then at what time will all Tathāgatas ever again produce any afflictions?"
2. The explanation by means of the analogy of the Tathāgata has two parts:
first, the explanation in terms of the gate of True Suchness (tathatā);
second, the explanation in terms of the gate of Arising and Ceasing (utpāda-nirodha).

The first gate dissolves appearances to reveal reality; thus, by means of the metaphors of losing one's direction and flowers in the sky, it is shown that ignorance, the mountains, rivers, and so forth have never arisen from the beginning and their substance cannot be apprehended. Although arising and ceasing appear due to the cataracts of a deluded mind, the true directions and empty space remain utterly unmoved.
The deluded mind and deluded objects appear to undergo arising and ceasing, yet how could the true, wondrous, enlightened clarity ever change?

The next section concerns the formation of phenomena by grasping at principle; thus, it uses the metaphors of gold from ore and ash from wood—both of which can be refined and burned—to illustrate the perfection of the fruit and the extinction of afflictions.
Although the two sections and four analogies differ from one another, they all demonstrate that after awakening, one no longer falls into delusion.
The first section has two parts:
first, the analogy of the square clearing away confusion to show that ignorance is fundamentally empty; second:
I. The Correct Analogy, in two parts: A.
Questioning and Answering Regarding Delusion About the Original Absence of Causes.
The Buddha addressed Pūrṇa:
“Suppose, for example, there is a person who has lost their way in a village and mistakes south for north.
Does this delusion arise because of further delusion, or does it emerge through awakening? Pūrṇa replied:
"In this way, the deluded person does not exist because of delusion, nor because of awakening.
Why is this? Delusion has no fundamental root; how, then, could one be deluded because of it?"
Awakening is not produced from delusion; how, then, could it be caused by awakening?
A gathering of people can be inhabited, hence it is called a "village" (grāma).
Deluded people are sentient beings.
The village is the Tathāgatagarbha.
"South" signifies the luminous nature;
"North" signifies that which is illuminated.
Delusion is ignorance (*avidyā*).
Although the southern aspect is immovable, because of delusion one perceives it as north; its nature is luminous and unchanging, yet through confusion one establishes an objective referent.
Since this delusive fantasy has emerged, I now investigate it to cause you to know that non-arising is itself seeing—that ignorance is fundamentally empty.
2. Question and Answer on Not Erring After Awakening.
The Buddha said:
"While that deluded person is in the midst of delusion, suddenly there is one who awakens who points it out and causes him to awaken."
Pūrṇa! What do you think? Even if this person were deluded, would he become further deluded within this village?
"No, World-Honored One! One who has attained awakening is a virtuous friend."
"Instruction" refers to teaching one to practice.
"Causing awakening" refers to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions.

Because Pūrṇa had doubts regarding the Dharma but attained clear understanding through metaphors, the Buddha raised a metaphor as a question to enable him to understand that the Dharma is like the metaphor.
2. Combined Manifestation.
"Pūrṇa! The Tathāgatas of the ten directions are likewise thus: this delusion has no fundamental basis; its nature is ultimately empty."
"Originally there was no delusion; it is only as if there were a perception of delusion. When one awakens from delusion, the delusion is extinguished; once awakened, delusion does not arise.
Delusion is ignorance (*avidyā*), which is also called folly (*moha*) and non-awakening (*abodhi*).

Awakening occurs precisely where there was no prior awakening; therefore, it is said that the nature is ultimately empty. From the perspective of the True Suchness gate (*tathatā-mukha*), there was originally no delusion; from the perspective of the Arising and Ceasing gate (*utpāda-nirodha-mukha*), delusion and awakening appear to exist.
Awakening is precisely the fundamental awakening that was the object of delusion;

it is also what is called initial awakening (*ādikṣaya-bodhi*). Regarding "awakening to delusion so that delusion is extinguished": when the wisdom of initial awakening arises, one awakens to the exhaustion of beginningless deluded thoughts. When this merges with fundamental awakening, there is no longer any distinction between the initial and the fundamental; there is only the single wondrous awakening. How could it give rise to delusion again?
Therefore, it is said that awakening does not give rise to delusion.
Second, the analogy of the disappearance of flowers when the cataract is cured, illustrating that the mountains, rivers, and so forth are unreal; this has two parts:
first, the question and answer based on the analogy; second, [the explanation]. First: the question and answer based on the analogy.
First, the question of the deluded person awaiting flowers:
"It is like a person with cataracts who sees flowers in the sky; once the disease of the cataracts is removed, the flowers vanish from the sky.
Suddenly, there is a foolish person who, in that empty space where the flowers have vanished, waits for the flowers to reappear."
"Do you consider this person to be foolish or wise?
The cataract serves as a metaphor for deluded vision, and the flowers serve as a metaphor for mountains and rivers.

When deluded vision ceases, the mountains and rivers naturally vanish; thus, the subsequent passage says: "Seeing and hearing are like illusory cataracts; the three realms are like flowers in the sky. When hearing is restored and the cataracts of the sense-faculties are removed, the dust of phenomena vanishes and awareness becomes perfectly pure."
Because there are no flowers in emptiness, it is called "empty ground.
Second, the answer from one who is inverted, mad, and deluded. Pūrṇa said:

"Empty space fundamentally has no flowers; it is through deluded vision that they arise and perish. To perceive the extinction of the flowers and take that to be empty space is already an inversion. To then command them to appear once more is truly madness. How can such a madman be called either ignorant or wise?"

The true source is signless, yet deluded views arise and cease. To perceive the extinction of mountains and rivers is already a perverted view; to wait for them to arise again is the same as being a madman.
2. Refutation by Counter-Interrogation and Conclusion.
The Buddha said:
"It is as you understand it."
Why do you ask: "Since the Buddhas and Tathāgatas possess wondrous, enlightened, luminous emptiness, when will mountains, rivers, and the great earth ever emerge again?
According to your understanding of this analogy, it is inconsistent for you to further doubt that the Tathāgata’s empty enlightenment gives rise to mountains and rivers.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "The Buddha teaches the abandonment of lust, anger, and delusion for those with overweening pride;
if there is no overweening pride, the Buddha teaches that the very nature of lust, anger, and delusion is liberation."
Thus one knows that through diligent effort as if in a dream, the delusion of empty names is severed; once the causes of illusion are fulfilled, the fruit of the mirror-image is perfected.
All instances of severance and realization should be understood according to this principle.
2. Explanation according to the gate of arising and ceasing, in two parts:
1. Simile, in two parts: 1. Simile for the accomplishment of the fruit.
"Furthermore, it is like gold ore mixed with refined gold; once the gold is pure, it can no longer be mixed again.
The awakening of sentient beings is obscured, like gold mixed with ore, while the awakening of the Buddhas is manifest, like pure gold."
Having already entered the ocean of fruition, it no longer serves as a cause; therefore, it is said that they do not again become intermingled.
Although cause and effect differ, the nature of awakening is equal.
Second, the metaphor for the extinction of delusion.
"Just as wood turned to ash cannot again become wood:

the nature of awakening is like the earth, delusive obstructions are like the wood, preparatory application is like the fire-drill, the illumination of wisdom is like the fire, and nirvāṇa is like the ash."
When the fire is struck from the flint and arises, the wood is exhausted and turns to ash; the ash returns to the earth and does not again become wood.
When the wisdom of cultivation arises, delusion is extinguished and awakening manifests; where it manifests is only the True, and delusion does not arise again.
2. Synthesis: "The bodhi and nirvāṇa of all Buddha-Tathāgatas are likewise so.
This synthesizes the two metaphors: the fruit of wisdom, which is bodhi, and the fruit of cessation, which is nirvāṇa.

However, among the four preceding metaphors, two pairs share the same intent. The first pair addresses the principle of perfect enlightenment: both sentient beings and Buddhas are equally the original reality. This establishes the preceding text’s point that all things are pure and fundamental, being entirely the Tathāgata-garbha, neither increasing nor decreasing relative to the mind of the Tathāgata. Therefore, it is cited that losing one's way and the flowers in the sky have never arisen from the beginning, nor do they cease only later;
thus, the Dharma correspondence states: "This delusion has no foundation; its nature is ultimately empty."
It further states:
"In emptiness there are fundamentally no flowers; it is through deluded vision that they appear and perish.
This implies that even for Pūrṇa to perceive the extinction of what is falsely existent is already an inversion; how much more so, then, to wait for the re-arising of residual outflows?

Subsequently, in order to clarify the characteristics of the cause and effect of cultivation and realization without regression, it is said that ore must be smelted to produce gold and wood must be burned to become ash.

While the confusion of directions and the flowers in the sky have been fundamentally non-existent from the beginning, gold and ash only manifest through smelting and burning; the meaning is that although the principle of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching is uniform, delusion and awakening may nonetheless differ. Since there are habitual obstructions accumulated over many lifetimes, one must turn away from those habits to reveal the Truth. Once the Truth is revealed, one is ultimately pure and will never again fall into delusion.
If one employs only the first two metaphors, one would negate the characteristics of the causes and effects of delusion and enlightenment, thereby constituting a false view.

If one employs only the latter two metaphors, it would follow that the awakened nature of sentient beings is inherently impure; this would deviate from the principle of true permanence and likewise constitute a false view.

The principle is subtle and profound; a single analogy is difficult to apply perfectly. Therefore, four matters are taught, each illustrating one dharma, in order to exhaustively clarify this principle.

"Pūrṇa! Furthermore, you asked: [the rest of the question follows]"

Furthermore, it is questioned how empty space and the great earth, both of which pervade the dharma-realm, can coexist without conflict.
Having previously raised a doubt, it is now being answered and explained; therefore, this is cited.
